nodes.text:
# Brief reader

Reads: pdf-to-md

The checklist belongs to the brief, not to one version, so it is written once and reused. If `checklist.md` lies next to the brief's Markdown in the project's `brief/` and is newer than every Markdown there, copy it into `brief-reader/` in the proposal folder you are told, write `summary.md`, and stop.

Otherwise read the brief's Markdown in parts, never all at once: list its headings and page markers (`<!-- page N -->`) with `grep`, then read the pages that hold the task, the programme, the rules, the submission and the jury's criteria. Write `checklist.md` next to the brief, in this order, one line per item, each ending with its source as `(<file> p. N)`:

- `## Numbers`: homes, residents, areas per use, green per resident, phases, and every other figure the design must meet.
- `## Rules`: heights, setbacks, what must stay, what is not wanted.
- `## Drawings and scales`: every drawing asked for, with its scale.
- `## Panels and format`: how many panels, their size and orientation, the texts and their length.
- `## Required content`: a numbered list of every item the brief requires on the panels or in the text, in the brief's words.
- `## What the jury looks for`: the criteria, as the brief states them.
- `## Pages`: each topic above and the pages to open for it, so other skills read only those.

Copy it into `brief-reader/` in the proposal folder. Never invent: what the brief doesn't say is written as "not stated". `summary.md`: three lines, the size of the task in one sentence, the number of required items, and what the brief leaves unclear.

# Narrative

Reads: brief-reader, analysis, climate
Reads (end): everything
Model: opus

This skill runs twice: first it builds the conceptual framework the project grows from, then it writes the text that explains the finished project. Work in the proposal folder you are given and write only into `narrative/`. Read the brief's checklist (`brief-reader/checklist.md`), `analysis/` and `climate/`; if one is missing, use the brief's Markdown and the site folder, and say so in `summary.md`. Never invent a fact: every claim names its file and, where there is one, the brief's page. Everything about the competition and the place comes from the brief.

**First run: the framework.** It must be memorable and solve a conflict, and it may be bold and abstract. Answer from the brief and the analysis what the project is for, who will use it and what it should say. Draft three stories in words, each with a different character (the site, its users or an abstract theme): its desire, the conflict in its way, and the transformation the design brings. Where no character comes naturally, use concept, angle and object. Choose the strongest, check that it doesn't restate the brief's own plan if the brief shows one, and add a move of your own that can be drawn and counted. The other skills design from this, so keep it clear. Write `narrative.md`:

- **Story:** the three answers, the three drafts in one sentence each, the chosen one and why, and its character, desire, conflict and transformation.
- **Title and subtitle:** short and memorable, not a slogan; the subtitle at most about eight words.
- **Idea:** one clear sentence without jargon, a paragraph on why this site asks for it, and your own move.
- **Principles:** three to five, one line each, that the design skills can check (where green runs, how dense, how people move). A principle may set its own target, marked as one.
- **Storyline:** one section per panel, in the number and format the checklist gives: its message in one line, and the drawings that carry it, named by the existing skills that make them.
- **Jury:** each criterion from the checklist and where the storyline answers it, or "open" or "partly open".

**Second run: the text.** Read every `summary.md` and table in the proposal folder. Write `text.md` for the jury, explaining the finished project in sequence: the idea, the concept, how it was built up (structure, programme, buildings, open space, movement, phases) and how it was approached (what the site showed, what was decided and why). Fit it into the brief's headings, length and language where the brief sets them, and put any other text it asks for, such as a short one for publication, in a file of its own. Give each key figure its source file in a footnote, and leave out figures that don't exist. Leave `narrative.md` as it is: the drawings were made from it. If the design has moved away from the framework, tell it in `text.md` and name the gap in `summary.md`.

**After each run**, write `summary.md` in three lines: the title and the idea in one sentence; the number that matters most to the idea, with its source; what you are least sure of.

# Programme

Reads: brief-reader

1. Read the brief checklist written by `brief-reader` in the proposal folder you are told, else the newest one. If it is missing, read the brief's Markdown in the project's `brief/`; if a figure is in neither, ask or say so in `summary.md`.
2. Take from the brief everything it asks to build, and table it:
   - **Homes and households:** the number of homes or the housing floor area, the household mix and unit types, and the residents. Where the brief gives a total but no mix, say so and leave the mix open; never invent shares.
   - **Uses and their areas:** commerce and ground-floor uses, schools and daycares with their capacity and outdoor space, community and sport, and anything else the brief lists, each with its gross floor area and plot.
   - **Shared and productive space:** uses shared by day and night, gardens and urban agriculture, shared amenities, only where the brief asks for them or gives a number.
3. Never invent data: next to every number, its source in the brief (with its page) or the assumption behind it, such as m² per resident. No drawings; text and tables only.
4. Write everything into `programme/` in the proposal folder and nothing outside it:
   - `programme.csv`: `use, area_m2, plot_m2, homes, residents, source`, one row per use, so `massing` can check its floor area against it.
   - `households.csv`: `household, share, homes, source`, if the brief gives a mix.
   - `programme.md`: what the brief asks for in words, and its open questions.
5. Create a `summary.md` of exactly three lines:
   - What you tabled.
   - The one key number that matters (total homes).
   - The one assumption or uncertainty you're highlighting.

# Structure plan

Reads: narrative, climate
Model: opus

Work in the proposal folder you are given and write only into `structure-plan/`. Take the idea from `narrative/`, the corridors to keep open from `climate/`, the site and its layers from the project's site folder, and the brief's checklist and the site analysis from `brief-reader/` and `analysis/` where they exist, else from the brief's Markdown; name each missing input in `summary.md`. If there is no site, ask for it. Work on `site.geojson` as it is; where it disagrees with the brief's plans, say so in `summary.md`. This is a framework, not a masterplan: stop at neighbourhoods, centres, green, routes and gateways, and leave buildings, street widths, hubs, planting and detail areas to the skills that follow.

Start from what is there: what to keep, then what to change, and only then what is new. Read the site's barriers, arrival points, existing destinations and the landscape beyond its boundary, and answer each: bridge or hold an edge, open a gateway where a route, a stop or a landscape meets the site, and continue the surrounding streets and paths into it. Divide the site into neighbourhoods by their existing spatial qualities (landscape, fabric, edges, relations) and name them by these, never by assumed residents or lifestyles. Place a main centre and local centres where the narrative and the site point, existing destinations among them, so that no single centre carries everything and a walk leads from one place to the next. Give green areas real extent and their roles (ecology, water, climate, recreation), combining roles in one area only where the site shows they are compatible, and keep climate corridors and green free of neighbourhoods.

Write `structure-plan.geojson` in WGS84, longitude first. Every feature has `kind`, `name`, `action` (keep, change or new), `basis` (documented, brief, mapped or hypothesis) and `source` where there is one:

- `neighbourhood` (polygon), which massing fills with buildings
- `centre` (polygon), `level` main or local
- `green` (polygon), `roles` as a list
- `route` (line), `level` main, local or landscape
- `gateway` (point), where the site meets the city or the landscape

Don't copy the site's layers. Check the geometry with `shapely` and `pyproj` (`pip install shapely pyproj`) in a metric projection; no Rhino, no drawings. Write `summary.md` in three lines: the figure in one sentence; the share of neighbourhood area within a distance you state of a centre or green, measured along routes where the site has a path network, else labelled as straight-line proximity, not walking access; the hypothesis that matters most and what evidence would settle it.

# Jury

Reads: brief-reader, panel-layout, narrative
Model: opus

Work in the proposal folder you are given, else the newest in the project's `proposals/`; write only to its `jury/`. Read every panel as an image, the plans up close, then `narrative/`, the checklist in `brief-reader/` and the brief (where the project's `CLAUDE.md` says, else `brief/`). With no panels, say so in `summary.md` and give no verdict. Judge only what the entry shows and the brief says, and never look up results or other entries. Trust the drawing over the caption: what the text promises and the plan doesn't show is missing. Recompute the entry's numbers against the brief's exact requirement, compare its figure and boundary with the brief's plans, and cite a panel or brief page for each claim.

Write `report.md` in the brief's language, as a Swiss jury report cut down to one entry, in the jury's sober voice ("is missed", "is questioned", "fails to fully convince"), with no contents page, member list, thanks or signatures:

1. **Task and criteria:** the task briefly, then the brief's criteria. They are rarely weighted, so the jury weights them itself before judging and says why, as carrying, contributing or supplementary, never in percentages. Weights the brief gives apply.
2. **Preliminary check:** without judgement, in tables: formal requirements, required contents, material requirements. Then the jury decides on admission; gaps don't exclude automatically.
3. **Rounds:** hurdles, following the brief's procedure where it has one, because one entry can't be compared. Say which it passes, where it is eliminated and why, and end with a control round that tests bringing it back.
4. **Appraisal:** continuous prose. Start with the siting, name strengths before doubts, give the key figures a paragraph, end on one or two overall sentences.
5. **Verdict:** in the brief's award levels, with no ranking.
6. **Recommendations for further work:** a list of tasks, also for an eliminated entry.

Unless the brief weights its criteria otherwise, test every entry hardest on its interior: how its buildings work inside or, at a larger scale, how its blocks and uses are organised. Where the panels don't show it, say so. A winner's interior goes uncriticised because it held and set the standard for the rest, so a quiet report means it passed, not that nobody looked. Open space ranks below the interior and may be average: it draws criticism often, is probably resolved only in further work, and never stops an entry from winning. Where open space is the idea, a plan that doesn't show it still counts against the concept. Also judge the unwritten criteria: self-evidence, fit with the place, and whether a political majority could back it. Mark these as assessments, supported by the entry and the brief. End with `summary.md` in three lines: the verdict and round; the number that weighed most; what you're unsure of.

# Panel layout

Reads: everything

Work in the proposal folder you are given, else the newest in the project's `proposals/`, else a new `proposals/<YYYY-MM-DD>_draft/`, never the project's top folder; write only to its `panel-layout/`. Needs Python 3.11+ and Chrome, Edge or Chromium (no other installs). First run `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/panels.py" scan <proposal folder>`: it lists every summary, drawing (with its print size and the scale its skill gives), table and text, and the inputs that are missing. Read every `summary.md`, the storyline and title from `narrative/`, and the format from `brief-reader/checklist.md`. If there is no checklist, read the format from the brief itself (where the project's `CLAUDE.md` says, else `brief/`): panel size and count, orientation, file limit, reserved boxes such as a code field, panel numbers, names and titles that must appear, the drawings and figures it asks for, and its language. Read the whole brief for these, not only its general submission rules: a site's own list of drawings, scales and figures often comes later, in the task or an appendix. Open every PNG before you finish: labels that overlap, a ground line that is missing, or buildings that float are mistakes.

**What to write**, into `site-section/` in the proposal folder: `site-section_<scale>.svg` and `.png` for the whole cut, `site-section_excerpt_<scale>.svg` and `.png`, `profile.csv`, and `summary.md` in three lines. Write the scale in a file name as `1-2000`, and give each SVG its width and height in mm at its scale, so it prints true to scale. The summary's three lines: what you drew and at which scales, the height difference along the cut, what you are unsure of.

# Climate

Reads: pdf-to-md, site-kit

This skill describes the place, then says what that asks of the design. Read the brief's Markdown and pictures for climate or fresh air maps, traffic counts, speeds, noise studies and noise limits, and the project's site folder (`site.geojson`, buildings, streets, rail, plots). Work in the proposal folder you're given and write only into `climate/`. Never invent data: every number carries its source (brief page, dataset, year) or is named as an assumption, and what can't be backed is left out and named in `summary.md`. Each step is a script in `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/`, run as `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/<script>.py" --site <site folder> --out <proposal>/climate`; `--help` explains each. Needs `pip install shapely pyproj numpy requests pillow pymupdf tzdata`, and Chrome or Edge for the PNGs.

1. **Fresh air** (`fresh_air.py`). If the brief has a climate map: `page` extracts it; pick three or more street crossings you can see on the map and in reality (`crossing` gives their coordinates), `fit`, and open `fit-check.png`: the site's streets must lie on the map's streets, about 100 m off is normal for a small map. Read its legend (if the brief has none, say so). In `classes.json` give each corridor as `at_px`, a pixel in its strongest colour: pale tints of that colour around it are not corridor. Give the arrows as colour ranges with the way they point as you see it, `trace`, and open `trace-check.png`: the green outline must follow only the corridor band. A WARNING means the colour caught too much or nothing; pick again. Without a map, `derive` from terrain and say there is no study.
2. **Sun** (`sun.py`): sun positions, shadows at 9, 12 and 15 h on 21 March and 21 December, and annual sun hours and radiation from an EPW weather file, so clouds count. It takes an `.epw` from the site folder if there is one, else a typical year from PVGIS.
3. **Wind** (`wind.py`): ten years of hourly wind, as a rose for the year, winter and summer.
4. **Noise** (`noise.py`): write `noise-sources.json` from the brief: each road with its daily traffic, speed and class, or an emission level from a noise study, each with its source; leave out what has no numbers and name it. Buildings screen the noise. The railway is optional: give its trains per day from the brief, a study or the site folder (in the sources file, or `--rail-trains N --rail-source "..."`); without them it stays off and the maps say so. Never assume train numbers outside a test, and mark a test value ASSUMED.
5. **Heat** (`heat.py`): a heat-island index from what covers the ground (roofs, roads, land use, trees, water) in the site folder; relative, not a temperature.
6. **Rules** (`rules.py`): put the brief's or the country's noise limits in `thresholds.json` with their source; without them it uses the German DIN 18005 and says so; the noise method (RLS-90, Schall 03) is German too, so on a site elsewhere say that in `summary.md`. It writes where not to build homes, where only behind a shielding edge, which corridors to keep open, which way to orient streets, and the wind notes. It also writes `climate.json`, the file for the design skills: the DON'T, CAREFUL and DO zones as GeoJSON polygons with the rule and its reason, and the key numbers.
7. **Drawings** (`draw.py`): the look comes from `drawing-graphics/` in the proposal folder (its `style.json`, else the colours and font named in `standard.md`), else black on white with one accent; check `drawings.txt` says which. Take the scale from the brief's checklist (`--scale`). Every map has a legend, north arrow, scale bar and sources. Open every PNG; fix what overlaps or reads wrong. After writing `summary.md`, run `draw.py --sheet` for `climate_sheet`: all maps on one A3 sheet with the summary.

Then write `climate.md`, one page: for each topic what it shows on this site and which parts it constrains, each line with its file or brief page, then the rules, then sources and licences (Open-Meteo CC BY 4.0, PVGIS © EU, OpenStreetMap ODbL). And `summary.md`, three lines: what you made, the one number that matters most (such as the share of the site too loud for homes), what you are least sure of. To check a design, run `sun.py` and `noise.py` again with `--buildings <its buildings>` into `climate/design/`.

# Site kit

Reads: nothing

Never hard-code a site, a city or a bounding box in this skill or in a script it makes; take the name, the stated area and the maps from the brief you are given. Never invent data. If a layer can't be found, leave it out and say so in `summary.md`.

**Where to look.** Collect the project site plus a margin wide enough for the smallest-scale drawing the brief asks for: a figure-ground at 1:15,000 on a 30 cm square needs about 2 km on every side; otherwise about 600 m. Go further if the brief names neighbours that lie further out, such as a station or a commercial area. Use OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API (`https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter`, try a mirror if it is busy) for buildings, streets, landuse, water and rail. For heights, try the state's open 3D building data (in Bavaria LoD2, in Thuringia LoD2 from GDI-Th) first, then `height` and `building:levels` tags in OSM. Where neither exists, use a stated default per building type (for example 2 floors for houses, 1 for halls) and flag it in the data with `height_source`. For the street land, try the open cadastre or land-use map (in Germany the state's ALKIS actual land use, with its streets, squares and paths as areas; elsewhere often the INSPIRE cadastral parcels, where the street is the land no plot covers).

**Finding the boundary.** If the brief gives a polygon or coordinates, use them. If it only shows the site on a map, render that page, locate the area on OpenStreetMap (match rail lines, main roads, forest edges and settlement edges), fit the map to coordinates, trace the marked outline and snap it to roads, rail or field edges where it follows them. Then check the area against any figure in the brief. State how close it is and how sure you are; a traced boundary is rarely better than 30 to 50 m.

**What to write.** Everything into the project's site folder: the one you're told, else where the project's `CLAUDE.md` says, else `site/` at the top. The site belongs to the project, not to one version, so every version reads the same data. If the folder already has a `site.geojson`, ask before you replace it.

- `site.geojson`: one polygon, WGS84, longitude first, `kind: "site"`.
- `buildings.geojson`: `height`, `floors`, `use`, `height_source`.
- `plots.geojson`: `landuse` (OSM landuse, natural and leisure polygons).
- `streets.geojson`, `water.geojson`, `rail.geojson`: lines, with names and types where known.
- `street-land.geojson`, if the cadastre has it: polygons, `use` street, square or path, `name`, `source`.
- `kit.json`: `label`, `center`, `bbox` (west, south, east, north), `size_m`, `generated`.
- `SOURCES.md`: each file, its source and licence (OSM is ODbL), the attribution line, and every default you applied.
- `summary.md`: three lines. What you collected, the site area in ha, what you are unsure of.

# PDF to Markdown

Reads: nothing, only the PDFs in the project

Much of what a project needs comes as PDF: the brief, a development plan, a traffic or noise study, city statistics, a reference project. The other skills read text. This skill converts each PDF with Docling, which keeps headings, lists and tables in reading order, so a number in a table stays next to its label. A marker `<!-- page N -->` stands before each page, so whoever takes a number from it can cite the file and the page.

Convert the PDFs the user names, or else every PDF in the project that has no Markdown yet. Write each result next to its PDF, so every version of a proposal reads the same text. For each: `python "${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/pdf_to_md.py" <pdf> <the PDF's folder>/ --images`. Add `--ocr` only if a page comes out empty but has text in the PDF, a scan. It writes `<name>.md` and the pictures (maps, plans, drawings, photos) at 300 dpi to `<name>-images/`, named by page, leaving out icons and logos under 3 cm. Plans and maps drawn in vectors also go to `<name>-drawings/` with the legend beside them, as PDF, SVG and PNG (`pip install pymupdf`). The first run downloads Docling's models, about 500 MB. If Docling isn't installed: `pip install docling`.

Then read each result against its PDF on a few pages with tables or key numbers. Fix nothing by hand. Next to each, write `<name>-summary.md`, one page at most, from its Markdown: what the document is and from whom, then what matters most in it (the task, key numbers and areas, dates, what it requires), each line with its page `(p. N)`. Only what it says; add nothing. Keep an `index.md` in the same folder, one line per PDF: where it came from, what it is, its pages. Write `summary.md` next to it, in three lines: which PDFs were converted, how many pages and tables, and any page that came out wrong or empty.
